Interest paid out or compounded: chart the cash received, spent and retained

Compare two hypothetical fixed-rate certificates with the same principal and term, while tracking the outside saving and consumption of annual interest payments.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore annual interest payments, outside saving and compounding

Interactive planning lab

Compounding choice: resources at maturity$60,832.65
Annual-payout choice: resources retained at maturity$55,204.04
Annual-payout interest already spent$5,000

Hypothetical fixed-rate certificates with identical initial principal, annual rate and maturity. One compounds annually to maturity; the other pays simple annual interest at year-end. The payout choice spends the selected share and saves the remainder outside at a separate annual rate. Outside interest accrues before the next year-end deposit. Principal returns at maturity in both choices. All amounts are before taxes and fees; no actual issuer, deposit-insurance status, early access or guaranteed reinvestment rate is established. Spending is consumption, not investment underperformance.

The central idea

A payment schedule and a retained-wealth comparison answer different questions. Interest spent on a bill is no longer an asset, and paid interest earns compound growth only when it is retained and reinvested.

01

Keep the principal, rate and maturity the same

A fixed-rate certificate can supply periodic interest or accumulate interest until maturity. The timing affects the cash a household receives before the term ends. It can also affect the resources retained when paid interest is spent or saved elsewhere.

The example starts both choices with CAD 50,000, a hypothetical 4% annual rate and a five-year maturity. One pays CAD 2,000 at the end of every year. The other adds annual interest to the certificate and pays its accumulated amount only at maturity. These are invented terms, not available rates or issuer quotations.

The Autorité des marchés financiers’ debt-securities overview describes periodic and compound interest structures for GICs. Actual contracts need their own interest calculation, payment schedule and access conditions. The examples here assume annual calculation and make no claim about deposit-insurance eligibility or an issuer’s particular certificate.

02

Read the payment bars before interpreting a yield

The annual-payout choice supplies CAD 2,000 at each of the first four year-ends. In year five, it pays CAD 2,000 of interest and returns CAD 50,000 of principal, producing a CAD 52,000 cash receipt on that date.

The compounding choice supplies no earlier cash under this assumed contract. At maturity, it pays CAD 50,000 × 1.045 = CAD 60,832.65, allowing for displayed rounding. The maturity bars include capital being returned; they are not measures of that year’s interest yield.

A household that needs cash in year two cannot automatically spend the accrued amount shown on the compounding line. The graph records an accumulated contract value, not an early-redemption price or a promise of access. Match a real spending deadline to confirmed payment dates and redemption provisions.

03

Give each annual interest payment an explicit destination

The default annual-payout choice spends half of each CAD 2,000 interest payment and saves the other half outside the certificate. That means CAD 1,000 of consumption and CAD 1,000 of outside saving at each year-end.

The outside account earns an assumed 2% annually before the next year-end deposit. Its first CAD 1,000 deposit receives no additional growth at the instant it arrives. Earlier deposits receive more years of outside interest than later ones, and the final deposit arrives at maturity with no subsequent year of growth inside the selected horizon.

After five years, the outside account holds about CAD 5,204.04. It consists of CAD 5,000 of saved certificate interest plus CAD 204.04 earned outside. Another CAD 5,000 of certificate interest has already been spent. The retained-resource line includes principal and outside savings, while keeping that past consumption separate.

04

Reconcile the resources without counting principal twice

The payout choice retains CAD 50,000 of principal plus CAD 5,204.04 outside savings, or CAD 55,204.04 at maturity. Its waterfall checks that result using original principal, all certificate interest paid, outside interest earned and consumption.

The reconciliation is CAD 50,000 + CAD 10,000 + CAD 204.04 − CAD 5,000 = CAD 55,204.04. Returning the original CAD 50,000 at maturity converts the certificate asset into cash; it does not create another CAD 50,000 of wealth alongside a continuing certificate asset.

The compounding choice retains CAD 60,832.65 and has funded no consumption in this example. Comparing that ending amount directly with CAD 55,204.04 includes a difference in spending as well as reinvestment. It would be misleading to describe the whole CAD 5,628.60 retained-resource gap as inferior investment performance.

05

Use the matrix to separate reinvestment from consumption

The matrix varies the outside account return and the share of paid interest spent. Each cell shows payout-choice resources minus compounding-choice resources at the common maturity. A negative cell can therefore arise because interest was consumed, because the outside rate was lower, or from both effects.

When no certificate interest is spent and the outside account earns the same 4% annual rate, the two choices finish with the same retained resources under these annual conventions. The certificate pays CAD 2,000 each year, and the separate account compounds those payments at the matching rate.

That equality is a mathematical control, not a promise that a matching reinvestment rate will be available. Outside rates can change and may involve different access conditions, taxes or risk. A higher assumed outside rate can increase the payout path’s endpoint, but the matrix assigns neither a likelihood nor a provider recommendation to any rate.

06

Add taxes, contract conditions and the household calendar separately

All amounts are before taxes and fees. The model does not determine tax recognition or payment dates for either structure, and it does not assume that receiving no cash automatically means having no tax obligation. The account wrapper and applicable rules need their own review.

Confirm whether a real certificate’s quoted rate, compounding convention and payment frequency match the example. Check the term, maturity instructions, early-redemption conditions and any renewal process. An outside account is a separate arrangement; its rate and availability should not be attributed to the certificate issuer without evidence.

Use the payment chart to plan cash receipts and the retained-resource ledger to explain what happened to interest after receipt. Then compare alternatives with the household’s actual spending needs stated consistently. Money already used to meet a bill has provided consumption, while money still held can fund a later need; the charts keep those roles distinct.
